The Bluespine unicornfish Naso unicornis exhibits a maximum total length of 70 centimeters [Li = 70 centimeters] in adult individuals, a size that distinguishes it as one of the larger members of the Acanthuridae family. This ultimate body length is attained only after many years of growth on coral reef habitats throughout the Indo-Pacific region, where these fish graze extensively on macroalgae. In contrast, the length at which individuals reach puberty is considerably smaller, with the transition to reproductive maturity occurring at a fork length of approximately 23.1 centimeters [Lp = approximately 23.1 centimeters]. This substantial difference between the size at maturation and the maximum attainable size suggests a prolonged period of adult growth following the onset of reproductive capability. Field surveys conducted across multiple reef sites indicate that the dietary shift from filamentous algae to larger brown algae species correlates with increasing body size, with the largest specimens often dominating the most productive foraging territories.

The maximum reproductive output of Bluespine unicornfish has been estimated under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]. At this thermal regime, females produce an estimated 3.44 million eggs per year [Ri = 3.44 million eggs per year], a figure that reflects the high fecundity characteristic of many pelagic-spawning teleosts. This annual fecundity is achieved through multiple spawning events throughout the year, with individual females releasing gametes during aggregation events that coincide with specific lunar phases. The high egg production compensates for the extremely small size of the offspring at the moment of hatching. When these values are considered in the context of the species' adult body mass, the reproductive allocation per unit of maternal tissue falls within the range observed for other large-bodied surgeonfishes that broadcast spawn in open water.

Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae of Naso unicornis emerge from pelagic eggs with a minute wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00023 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00023 grams]. This minuscule neonatal body mass, which corresponds to an egg diameter of roughly 0.75 millimeters, places the species among the teleosts that produce highly numerous but energetically inexpensive offspring. The lecithotrophic phase following eclosion lasts only a few days before the mouth opens and the prolarva must successfully capture its first planktonic prey. The transition to exogenous feeding is a critical bottleneck in the life cycle, as the tiny larvae possess limited yolk reserves and must locate suitable concentrations of microzooplankton to avoid starvation. Mortality during these early pelagic stages is exceptionally high, a demographic reality that necessitated the evolution of the species' characteristically high fecundity to ensure that at least a small fraction of offspring survive to settlement.

Adults of the Bluespine unicornfish reach an ultimate wet weight of roughly 10,418 grams [Wwi = roughly 10,418 grams], a massive body size that supports their foraging ecology on coral reefs. In contrast, the wet weight at puberty is substantially smaller, with individuals typically weighing approximately 446 grams [Wwp = approximately 446 grams] when they first become reproductively active. This dramatic increase in body mass from maturation to maximum size indicates that growth continues steadily throughout much of adult life, with the largest individuals often being the most successful in both territory defense and gamete production. The relationship between length and weight follows a predictable allometric curve typical of acanthurids, with mass increasing disproportionately as length approaches the species' asymptotic value. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Naso lituratus suggest that the Bluespine unicornfish invests heavily in somatic growth before and after maturity, a strategy that may enhance both competitive ability and lifetime reproductive success.

When maintained at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the Bluespine unicornfish exhibits a remarkable lifespan of approximately 30 years [am = approximately 30 years], placing it among the longer-lived members of the surgeonfish family. This extended longevity contrasts sharply with the extremely brief and vulnerable pelagic larval duration that precedes benthic settlement. The species' slow growth rate and delayed maturation relative to smaller acanthurids contribute to this extended lifespan, with adults experiencing relatively low natural mortality once they have recruited to reef habitats. Observations of tagged individuals on protected reef systems have confirmed that some fish survive well past the 20-year mark, continuing to spawn annually throughout their adult lives. The combination of high annual fecundity, extended reproductive lifespan, and the production of very small larvae represents a classic bet-hedging life history strategy well suited to the unpredictable survival conditions facing pelagic offspring in tropical reef ecosystems.
